summary: FieldShift is a free web tool that helps farmers in Finney County, Kansas, explore what a different crop rotation could do for their own center-pivot field as water from the Ogallala aquifer declines. A farmer picks a field on a satellite map and sees 18 years of its crop history and how many months it sat without green cover. They set five priorities (water, income, soil organic matter, erosion, labour) and how much water they can actually pump. FieldShift then compares their current rotation with three alternatives across 31 years of NASA weather. Results are ranges (a 1-in-10 low, typical and 1-in-10 high year), and each rotation shows how often it came out on top under the farmer's priorities, e.g. "on top in about 8 of 10 runs". It never says "plant X". Every result lists what to verify locally and what we don't know, and the farmer can print a one-page summary for their adviser. It uses NASA POWER, MODIS, GRACE/GRACE-FO and SRTM with process-based models (FAO-56, RUSLE), not black-box SI.
details:
What it does.

FieldShift turns NASA Earth observations into a per-field "passport" and a side-by-side comparison of four crop rotations for the 50 center-pivot fields of Finney County, Kansas (FIPS 20055). It takes four steps and needs no account:

  1. your field: crop history 2008–2025 from the USDA Cropland Data Layer, months without green cover from MODIS NDVI, soil, slope and heat-stress days;
  2. what matters to you: five priority sliders plus your realistic irrigation limit;
  3. compare: your detected rotation and three alternatives, as ranges;
  4. a printable one-page summary for the water district, K-State extension or NRCS.

How it works.

Field circles are delineated automatically from the CDL raster, and the current rotation is the shortest repeating crop cycle in the last 8 years. For each rotation we run a daily FAO-56 water balance (Penman-Monteith ET0 × crop coefficients, a soil water bucket from SSURGO, and center-pivot irrigation with an optional seasonal cap) on NASA POWER weather. Yield responds to water stress through FAO-33 Ky factors, and income uses K-State crop budgets and pumping costs. Water erosion comes from a simplified RUSLE (rainfall erosivity from POWER, soil erodibility from SSURGO, slope from SRTM), and the soil organic matter trend from an NRCS-style soil conditioning index. Each start year 1995–2025 gives one sample, so every metric is reported as p10/p50/p90. The ranking is a multi-criteria analysis with 2,000 Monte Carlo draws: priority weights are sampled from a Dirichlet distribution around the farmer's sliders and metrics from their intervals. "P(best)" is the share of draws in which a rotation scores highest. It is recomputed live in the browser as the sliders move. GRACE/GRACE-FO mascons show the regional water-storage trend (about −0.86 cm/yr since 2002) that motivates the tool.

Why it matters.

The Ogallala aquifer is being drawn down faster than it refills, and pumping limits are tightening. In our example field, adding a 14-inch water limit changes which rotation comes out on top (from alfalfa–corn in ~5 of 10 runs to sorghum–wheat–cover crop in ~8 of 10). The tool also shows the honest income cost of that change. FieldShift makes these trade-offs visible before a farmer commits a season, and it hands them to the adviser conversation rather than replacing it.

Honesty about uncertainty.

We show ranges, never single numbers, and never say "you should plant". Every rotation has a "what we don't know / verify locally" box. Known gaps are listed in the app: GRACE is a ~300 km regional signal, not a well; POWER weather is a ~50 km grid; wind erosion is not modelled; land rent and pivot/well costs are not subtracted; some parameters are placeholders.

Tools.

Python 3.11 (numpy, pandas, rasterio) for the offline data pipeline and models, all exported to static JSON/GeoJSON validated against JSON Schemas. Web app: TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL, deck.gl, Recharts, hosted on GitHub Pages with no server and no running costs. Any water district or extension office can host it for free.

Creativity and design choices.

Satellite data is translated into a farmer's own pivot, which they recognise by its roads. Uncertainty is shown as "N of 10 weather runs", a phrasing that can be read without statistics. Explainable process models were chosen over machine learning, because 31 seasons is too small a sample for that. The interface needs no account and is accessible, with large touch targets and plain language.
